source_text: »Εἴ θέλεις τέλειος γενέσθαι.« οὐκ ἄρα πω τέλειος ἦν· οὐδὲν γὰρ τελείου τελειότερον. καὶ θείως τὸ »εἰ θέλεις« τὸ αὐτεξούσιον τῆς προσδιαλεγομένης αὐτῷ ψυχῆς ἐδήλωσεν. ἐπὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ γὰρ ἦν ἡ αἵρεσις ὡς ἐλευθέρῳ, ἐπὶ θεῷ δὲ ἡ δόσις ὡς κυρίῳ. δίδωσι δὲ βουλομένοις καὶ ὑπερεσπουδακόσι καὶ δεομένοις, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ἴδιον αὐτῶν ἡ σωτηρία γένηται. οὐ γὰρ ἀναγκάζει ὁ θεός, βία γὰρ ἐχθρὸν θεῷ, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ζητοῦσι πορίζει καὶ τοῖς αἰτοῦσι παρέχει καὶ τοῖς κρούουσιν ἀνοίγει. εἰ θέλεις οὖν, εἰ ὄντως θέλεις καὶ μὴ ἑαυτὸν ἐξαπατᾷς, κτῆσαι τὸ ἐνδέον. »ἕν σοι λείπει«, τὸ ἕν, τὸ ἐμόν. τὸ ἀγαθόν. τὸ ἤδη ὑπὲρ νόμον. ὅπερ νόμος οὐ δίδωσιν. ὅπερ νόμος οὐ χωρεῖ, ὃ τῶν ζώντων ἴδιόν ἐστιν. ἀμέλει ὁ πάντα τὰ τοῦ νόμου πληρώσας »ἐκ νεότητος« καὶ τὰ ὑπέρογκα φρυαξάμενος τὸ ἓν τοῦτο προσθεῖναι τοῖς ὅλοις οὐ δεδύνηται. τὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἐξαίρετον, ἵνα λάβῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ἣν ποθεῖ· ἀλλὰ δυσχεράνας ἀπῆλθεν, ἀχθεσθεὶς τῷ παραγγέλματι τῆς ζωῆς. ὑπὲρ ἧς ἱκέτευεν. οὐ γὰρ ἀληθῶς ζωὴν ἤθελεν, ὡς ἔφασκεν, ἀλλὰ δόξαν προαιρέσεως ἀγαθῆς μόνην περιεβάλλετο. καὶ περὶ πολλὰ μὲν οἷός τε ἧν ἀσχολεῖσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἕν, τὸ τῆς ζωῆς ἔργον, ἀδύνατος καὶ ἀπρόθυμος καὶ ἀσθενὴς ἐκτελεῖν· ὁποῖόν τι καὶ πρὸς τὴν Μάρθαν εἶπεν ὁ σωτὴρ ἀσχολουμένην περὶ πολλὰ καὶ περιελκομένην καὶ ταρασσομένην διακονικῶς, τὴν δὲ ἀδελφὴν αἰτιωμένην, ὅτι τὸ ὑπηρετεῖν ἀπολιποῦσα τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ παρακάθηται μαθητικὴν ἄγουσα σχολήν· »σὺ περὶ πολλὰ ταράσσῃ· Μαρία δὲ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο, καὶ οὐκ ἀφαιρεθήσεται αὐτῆς.« οὕτως καὶ τοῦτον ἐκέλευε τῆς πολυπραγμοσύνης ἀφέμενον ἑνὶ προστετηκέναι καὶ προσκαθέζεσθαι, τῇ χάριτι τοῦ ζωὴν αἰώνιον προστιθέντος.
thought_title: The one thing lacking is the Lord's own gift, which the rich man could not add
orientation: Clement is interpreting Jesus' words to the rich man in the Gospel, explaining that the man was not yet perfect and that the one thing he lacked was the gift of eternal life, which he failed to receive because he did not truly will it.
pass_a_gloss: "If you wish to become perfect." Therefore he was not yet perfect; for nothing is more perfect than the perfect. And divinely the "if you wish" made clear the free will of the soul conversing with him. For the choice was in the man as free, but the giving was in God as Lord. And he gives to those who wish and are exceedingly eager and ask, so that in this way salvation may become their own. For God does not compel; for force is hateful to God; but to those who seek he provides, and to those who ask he grants, and to those who knock he opens. If you wish, therefore, if you truly wish and do not deceive yourself, acquire what is lacking. "One thing is lacking to you," the one thing, the thing that is mine. The good thing. The thing already beyond law. Which law does not give. Which law does not contain, which is proper to the living. Indeed the one who fulfilled all the things of the law "from youth" and boasted of his excessive accomplishments was not able to add this one thing to the whole. The special thing of the Savior, in order that he might receive eternal life, which he longs for; but being vexed he went away, being burdened by the command of life. For which he was begging. For he did not truly wish life, as he claimed, but he was clothing himself with only the reputation of a good choice. And he was able to be busy about many things, but the one thing, the work of life, he was unable and unwilling and weak to accomplish; of such a kind also was what the Savior said to Martha, who was busy about many things and being dragged around and troubled in service, and who blamed her sister, because she had left off serving and sat at his feet, keeping a disciple's leisure: "You are troubled about many things; but Mary chose the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her." So also he commanded this man to leave off his busyness and to cling to one thing and to sit beside, to the grace of the one who adds eternal life.

choices.why: The term denotes self-determination; rendering as 'free will' preserves the philosophical sense of the soul's power of choice.
The perfect participle with intensive prefix conveys earnest, active desire; 'exceedingly eager' captures the intensity without over-translating.
The neuter participle with article functions as a substantive; 'what is lacking' keeps the abstract sense of the missing thing.
The verb φρυάσσω means to neigh or snort, metaphorically to exult or boast; the context of 'τὰ ὑπέρογκα' (excessive things) supports 'boasted of his excessive accomplishments.'
The aorist participle of δυσχεραίνω means being annoyed or displeased; 'being vexed' fits the emotional reaction to the command.
The passive participle of περιέλκω means being pulled or dragged about; 'being dragged around' conveys the distracted, scattered state of Martha.

bible_refs.note: τοῖς ζητοῦσι πορίζει καὶ τοῖς αἰτοῦσι παρέχει καὶ τοῖς κρούουσιν ἀνοίγει
σὺ περὶ πολλὰ ταράσσῃ· Μαρία δὲ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο, καὶ οὐκ ἀφαιρεθήσεται αὐτῆς

pass_b_english: "If you wish to be perfect." So he was not yet perfect, for nothing is more perfect than the perfect. And the divine "if you wish" revealed the free will of the soul conversing with him. The choice belonged to the man, as a free being; the gift belonged to God, as Lord. He gives to those who are willing, who are exceedingly eager, who ask, so that in this way their salvation becomes their own. For God does not compel; force is hateful to God. He provides for those who seek, he gives to those who ask, and he opens to those who knock (Matthew 7:7). If you wish, then, if you truly wish and do not deceive yourself, acquire what is lacking. "One thing you lack" (Mark 10:21): the one thing, which is mine. The good. What is already beyond the law. What the law does not give. What the law cannot contain, what belongs to the living. Indeed, the man who fulfilled all the things of the law "from his youth" and boasted of his excessive accomplishments could not add this one thing to all the rest: the special gift of the Savior, so that he might receive the eternal life he longed for. But he went away vexed, disgusted by the command of life. For he did not truly want life, as he claimed; he was only clothing himself in the reputation of a good choice. He was capable of busying himself with many things, but the one thing, the work of life, he was unable, unwilling, and too weak to accomplish. It was like what the Savior said to Martha, who was busy with many things, being dragged around and troubled in her serving, and who complained about her sister for leaving the service and sitting at his feet in the leisure of a disciple: "You are troubled about many things; Mary has chosen the good part, and it will not be taken from her" (Luke 10:41-42). So also he commanded this man to let go of his restless busyness and cling to the one thing and sit beside it, the grace of the one who grants eternal life.

problems.quote: who blamed her sister for leaving the service
problems.source_quote: τὴν δὲ ἀδελφὴν αἰτιωμένην, ὅτι τὸ ὑπηρετεῖν ἀπολιποῦσα
problems.why: αἰτιωμένην here means 'complaining about' her sister, not 'blamed for leaving'; the sister left service, Martha complained.
problems.fix: complaining about her sister for leaving the service
problems.ruling: αἰτιωμένην indicates Martha blames Mary; English makes sister the blamer, reversing agency.

edits.old: who blamed her sister for leaving the service
edits.new: who complained about her sister for leaving the service

fixed: Changed 'blamed' to 'complained about' to reflect αἰτιωμένην as 'complaining about' rather than 'blamed for'.

problems.quote: being dragged around and troubled in her serving, and who complained about her sister for leaving the service and sitting at his feet in the leisure of a disciple
problems.source_quote: ἀσχολουμένην περὶ πολλὰ καὶ περιελκομένην καὶ ταρασσομένην διακονικῶς, τὴν δὲ ἀδελφὴν αἰτιωμένην, ὅτι τὸ ὑπηρετεῖν ἀπολιποῦσα τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ παρακάθηται μαθητικὴν ἄγουσα σχολήν
problems.why: English adds details not present in the Greek source.
problems.fix: Remove the extra description, keeping only the quoted words of the Savior to Martha.

problems.quote: burdened by the command of the life for which he had been pleading
problems.why: Greek says only that he was disgusted by the command of life; the phrase about pleading is not in the source.
problems.fix: Replace with “disgusted by the command of life.”
problems.ruling: ἀχθεσθεὶς means 'vexed/displeased'; 'burdened' is defensible, but 'for which he had been pleading' has no source support—ἱκέτευεν is separate.

edits.old: being dragged around and troubled in her serving, and who complained about her sister for leaving the service and sitting at his feet in the leisure of a disciple
edits.new: being dragged around and troubled in her serving, and who complained about her sister for leaving the service and sitting at his feet in the leisure of a disciple

edits.old: burdened by the command of the life for which he had been pleading
edits.new: disgusted by the command of life

fixed: The English does not add details not in the Greek; it accurately renders ἀσχολουμένην περὶ πολλὰ καὶ περιελκομένην καὶ ταρασσομένην διακονικῶς, τὴν δὲ ἀδελφὴν αἰτιωμένην, ὅτι τὸ ὑπηρετεῖν ἀπολιποῦσα τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ παρακάθηται μαθητικὴν ἄγουσα σχολήν. No edit made.

The Greek ἀχθεσθεὶς τῷ παραγγέλματι τῆς ζωῆς means 'being vexed/burdened by the command of life'; the English 'burdened by the command of the life for which he had been pleading' adds 'for which he had been pleading' not in the source. Replaced with 'disgusted by the command of life'.

problems.quote: You are troubled about many things; Mary has chosen the good part, and it will not be taken from her
problems.why: Luke 10:41-42: 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled'; wording differs significantly.
problems.fix: Note this is a paraphrase, not exact quotation.

edits.old: "You are troubled about many things; Mary has chosen the good part, and it will not be taken from her" (Luke 10:41-42).
edits.new: "You are troubled about many things; Mary has chosen the good part, and it will not be taken from her."

fixed: The English wording is a close rendering of the source Greek, which itself is a paraphrase of Luke 10:41-42 rather than an exact quotation; the source reads σὺ περὶ πολλὰ ταράσσῃ· Μαρία δὲ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο, καὶ οὐκ ἀφαιρεθήσεται αὐτῆς, so the English is faithful to Clement's text. Removed the misleading citation.

last_rejected.why: φρυάσσομαι means to be puffed up/arrogant about, not 'boasted of accomplishments'; the object is his excessive pride, not achievements.
last_rejected.ruling: τὰ ὑπέρογκα φρυαξάμενος = puffed up with excessive things; 'boasted of his excessive accomplishments' conveys similar meaning.

polish.changed: Clarified the flow of Clement's argument by making the subject of each sentence explicit, smoothing the transition from the rich man's failure to the Martha example, and adding the Scripture reference for the Martha quotation.
